title: 03. Databases & Data Modeling: Read Replicas
summary: Read replicas are copies of a primary database that serve read-only queries, scaling read throughput horizontally while the primary handles all writes — at the cost of eventual consistency (replication lag) and the…
objectives: What problem do read replicas solve and what's the trade-off?
What is the read-after-write problem and how do you solve it?
How do you route reads to replicas — what strategies exist?
How does Amazon Aurora's replication differ from PostgreSQL streaming replication?

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** Read replicas are copies of a primary database that serve read-only queries, scaling read throughput horizontally while the primary handles all writes — at the cost of **eventual consistency** (replication lag) and the **read-after-write** problem where a user writes to the primary then reads stale data from a replica.

Most production database workloads are read-heavy — typical ratios are 10:1 or 100:1 reads to writes. A single primary handling both reads and writes will saturate on reads long before writes become a bottleneck. Read replicas solve this by adding N read-only copies of the primary; reads distribute across them, write throughput stays bounded by the single primary, and total read capacity scales roughly linearly with replica count. The primary streams its WAL/binlog to the replicas asynchronously (Topic 13), so replicas are typically milliseconds to seconds behind the primary. This makes read replicas an **eventual consistency** mechanism: writes are immediately durable on the primary, but reads from replicas may return stale data for a brief window. The trade-off is fundamental: read scale requires accepting eventual consistency, and the engineering challenge is making that eventual consistency invisible to users who don't expect it.

The canonical read-replica topology is **one primary + N read replicas**. Writes go to the primary; the application routes reads based on consistency needs: "strong" reads (must see the latest write) go to the primary; "eventual" reads (a few seconds stale is OK) go to a replica chosen by load balancer (least connections, round-robin, or weighted). The routing decision is usually made by a connection pooler (PgBouncer, ProxySQL, HAProxy) or by application code using a "read-write session" vs "read-only session" abstraction. Modern ORMs (Django, SQLAlchemy, Hibernate) have built-in read-replica routing — you mark a query as read-only and the ORM picks a replica. The challenge is correctly classifying reads: a query that filters by `user_id` after the user just updated their profile is read-after-write and must go to the primary; a query that lists trending products can tolerate seconds of staleness and goes to a replica. Getting this wrong produces confusing UX bugs ("I updated my profile but it shows the old one").

The central problem is **read-after-write consistency** (also called read-your-writes). User A updates their profile picture (write to primary). User A's next page load reads the profile from a replica that's 200ms behind. The replica returns the old profile picture. User A is confused — "I just updated it, why does it show the old one?" Solutions: (1) **Pin reads to the primary for a duration after the user's write** — the application tracks `last_write_at` per session and routes the user's reads to the primary for the next N seconds (longer than expected replication lag). Simple and effective. (2) **Read-your-writes through the primary for the user's own data** — reads of "my profile" go to the primary; reads of "other users' profiles" go to replicas. (3) **Session consistency via replica LSN tracking** — the application records the LSN of the user's last write; subsequent reads go to a replica that has caught up to that LSN (PostgreSQL's `pg_wal_lsn_diff` lets you check). More complex but precise. (4) **Client-side cache invalidation** — the application caches the user's own writes locally for N seconds, bypassing the replica. (5) **Synchronous replication for the user's data** — overkill for most apps but used for critical data (e.g., a banking balance). Real-world: Facebook's "I just posted, why isn't it showing" bug in the early days led them to implement session-pinned reads for 30 seconds after a user's write.

Real-world: Amazon Aurora supports up to 15 read replicas sharing the same distributed storage as the primary. Adding a replica is instant — no data copy, because the storage layer is shared. Replicas have zero lag (they read the same shared storage), eliminating the read-after-write problem for Aurora specifically. This is a major architectural advantage over traditional PostgreSQL/MySQL where each replica has its own storage and lags behind. Aurora replicas still serve reads at the cost of compute (CPU, memory) but not storage or replication lag. Netflix uses Aurora with 10+ replicas for its movie metadata — the read load is enormous (every browse, search, recommendation triggers metadata reads), and Aurora's shared-storage replicas handle it without lag. The trade-off: Aurora is more expensive than vanilla PostgreSQL (proprietary storage, 6 copies of data) and the compute cost scales with replica count.

Real-world: Netflix's read-heavy query routing is a textbook example. Netflix's viewing history database receives 100k reads/sec (every "continue watching" list, every "you watched X" badge, every recommendation) and ~1k writes/sec (play/pause events). The primary handles 1k writes/sec comfortably; the 100k reads/sec are distributed across ~10 Cassandra replicas (RF=3, so 30 replica instances for 10 logical replicas). The routing layer uses consistency level `LOCAL_ONE` for reads (sub-millisecond, eventual consistency) and `LOCAL_QUORUM` for writes (strong consistency within the local DC). The read-after-write problem is solved by writing the user's last view position to a Redis cache (immediate read for the user's own "continue watching") while Cassandra is the durable store. The cache invalidates on TTL; the user always sees their latest position via Redis, and other users never see another user's position (so cross-user consistency doesn't matter).

Replica utilization patterns: (1) **Round-robin** — distribute reads evenly across replicas. Simple but doesn't account for replica-specific load. (2) **Least-connections** — route to the replica with the fewest active queries. Better load balancing but requires a stateful proxy. (3) **Latency-aware** — route to the replica with the lowest current lag. Useful when replicas have variable lag (e.g., one replica is also serving analytics). (4) **Workload-based** — OLTP queries go to fast replicas; analytical queries go to a dedicated "analytics replica" with more CPU but possibly more lag. (5) **Geography-based** — route reads to the nearest replica (cross-region read replicas for global apps). The choice depends on the workload heterogeneity. PgBouncer and ProxySQL support most of these; application-level routing gives the most control but is more code.

The operational concerns of read replicas: (1) **Replica lag monitoring** — alert if lag exceeds 1 second (async) or 100ms (sync). Long lag means stale reads and growing failover data loss. (2) **Replica failure handling** — if a replica goes down, the load balancer must reroute its traffic to other replicas; if all replicas are down, reads fall back to the primary (which may then be overloaded). (3) **Schema migrations** — the primary gets the new schema first; replicas must be migrated too. Online schema change tools (pg-osc, gh-ost) handle this without downtime. (4) **Connection limits** — each replica has its own connection pool; the pooler must respect per-replica limits. (5) **Long-running queries on replicas** — a slow analytical query on a replica can block WAL apply (single-threaded apply), increasing lag for all reads from that replica. Mitigation: isolate analytical queries to a dedicated replica. (6) **Failover** — when the primary fails, a replica is promoted; the other replicas must re-point to the new primary. Tools like Patroni handle this automatically.

Fix: pin user's reads to Primary for 5s after their write (or read from Primary for the user's own data always) Aurora (shared storage, 15 replicas, zero lag): +----------+ | Primary |---+ +----------+ | v +-----------+ | Shared | (6 copies across 3 AZs) | Storage | +-----+-----+ ^ +----------+ | +----------+ |Replica 1 |---+---|Replica 2 | ... (up to 15) +----------+ +----------+ (all read same storage -> zero lag, instant add) ``` ### Walkthrough 1. Writes flow to the primary, which commits locally and streams WAL asynchronously to N read replicas. Replicas apply the WAL with a small lag (milliseconds to seconds, depending on network and load). The primary acks the write to the client immediately, without waiting for replicas. 2. Read requests hit a router that classifies each read: "strong" reads (read-after-write, user's own data, financial) go to the primary; "eventual" reads (catalog, recommendations, analytics) go to a replica. The router may use round-robin, least-connections, or lag-aware routing to distribute load. 3. If a replica's lag grows (network issue, heavy load), the router can route around it. If the primary fails, a replica is promoted (failover) and the router updates to point writes at the new primary. Read replicas provide horizontal read scaling with eventual consistency, with the read-after-write problem solved via session pinning or routing the user's own data to the primary.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
**What this code covers**

- Read replica router with lag tracking and read-after-write protection.
- Routes reads with read-after-write protection.
- Simulate read latency + variable lag
- Read-after-write protection: if session recently wrote, use primary

**Defines:** `Replica`, `Primary`, `ReadRouter`

```python
"""
Read replica router with lag tracking and read-after-write protection.

Models:
  1. A primary + N read replicas, each with simulated lag
  2. A router that picks a replica based on routing strategy
  3. Read-after-write protection: pin to primary for N seconds after write
  4. Lag-aware routing: pick the replica with the lowest current lag

Run:  python3 read_replicas_demo.py
"""

import time
import random
import threading
from collections import defaultdict

class Replica:
    def __init__(self, name, base_lag_ms):
        self.name = name
        self.base_lag_ms = base_lag_ms
        self.current_lag_ms = base_lag_ms
        self.active_conns = 0
        self.alive = True

    def read(self):
        if not self.alive:
            raise RuntimeError(f"{self.name} down")
        self.active_conns += 1
        # simulate read latency + variable lag
        time.sleep(0.001)  # 1ms read
        self.current_lag_ms = self.base_lag_ms + random.randint(-10, 50)
        self.active_conns -= 1
        return {"served_by": self.name, "lag_ms": self.current_lag_ms}

class Primary:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
        self.lsn = 0   # log sequence number
        self.last_writer_sessions = {}  # session_id -> last_write_time

    def write(self, session_id, payload):
        self.lsn += 1
        self.last_writer_sessions[session_id] = time.time()
        time.sleep(0.005)  # 5ms write
        return {"lsn": self.lsn, "served_by": self.name, "lag_ms": 0}

    def read(self):
        time.sleep(0.005)  # 5ms (slower than replicas due to write load)
        return {"served_by": self.name, "lag_ms": 0}

    def session_recently_wrote(self, session_id, window_sec=5):
        t = self.last_writer_sessions.get(session_id, 0)
        return (time.time() - t) < window_sec

class ReadRouter:
    """Routes reads with read-after-write protection."""

    def __init__(self, primary, replicas, strategy="round_robin"):
        self.primary = primary
        self.replicas = [r for r in replicas if r.alive]
        self.strategy = strategy
        self.rr_idx = 0

    def route(self, session_id=None, strong=False):
        # Read-after-write protection: if session recently wrote, use primary
        if session_id and self.primary.session_recently_wrote(session_id):
            return self.primary.read(), "primary (read-after-write pin)"

        if strong:
            return self.primary.read(), "primary (strong read)"

        if self.strategy == "round_robin":
            r = self.replicas[self.rr_idx % len(self.replicas)]
            self.rr_idx += 1
            return r.read(), f"{r.name} (round-robin)"

        elif self.strategy == "least_connections":
            r = min(self.replicas, key=lambda x: x.active_conns)
            return r.read(), f"{r.name} (least-conn)"

        elif self.strategy == "lag_aware":
            r = min(self.replicas, key=lambda x: x.current_lag_ms)
            return r.read(), f"{r.name} (lag-aware, lag={r.current_lag_ms}ms)"

        raise ValueError(self.strategy)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    random.seed(42)

    primary = Primary("primary")
    replicas = [
        Replica("replica1", base_lag_ms=50),
        Replica("replica2", base_lag_ms=80),
        Replica("replica3", base_lag_ms=150),
    ]

    print("=== Round-robin routing ===")
    rr = ReadRouter(primary, replicas, strategy="round_robin")
    for i in range(6):
        r, why = rr.route()
        print(f"  read {i}: served_by={r['served_by']:<10} why={why}")

    print("\n=== Least-connections routing ===")
    rr = ReadRouter(primary, replicas, strategy="least_connections")
    for i in range(6):
        r, why = rr.route()
        print(f"  read {i}: served_by={r['served_by']:<10} why={why}")

    print("\n=== Lag-aware routing (picks lowest-lag replica) ===")
    rr = ReadRouter(primary, replicas, strategy="lag_aware")
    for i in range(6):
        r, why = rr.route()
        print(f"  read {i}: served_by={r['served_by']:<10} why={why}")

    print("\n=== Read-after-write protection ===")
    rr = ReadRouter(primary, replicas, strategy="round_robin")
    session = "user_alice"
    print(f"  Alice writes profile update...")
    primary.write(session, "new profile pic")
    print(f"  Alice's next 3 reads (should pin to primary):")
    for i in range(3):
        r, why = rr.route(session_id=session)
        print(f"    read {i}: served_by={r['served_by']:<10} why={why}")
    print(f"  ... 6 seconds later (pin expires) ...")
    time.sleep(6)
    print(f"  Alice's next read (should go to replica):")
    r, why = rr.route(session_id=session)
    print(f"    read: served_by={r['served_by']:<10} why={why}")

    print("\n=== Strong read (always primary) ===")
    r, why = rr.route(strong=True)
    print(f"  served_by={r['served_by']}, why={why}")

    print("\n=== Replica failure (router reroutes) ===")
    replicas[0].alive = False
    rr = ReadRouter(primary, replicas, strategy="round_robin")
    print(f"  replica1 marked down; reads now route to:")
    for i in range(4):
        r, why = rr.route()
        print(f"    read {i}: served_by={r['served_by']:<10} why={why}")

    print("\n=== Summary ===")
    print("  Read replicas scale reads horizontally (1 primary + N replicas)")
    print("  Lag varies per replica (ms to sec) -> eventual consistency")
    print("  Read-after-write: pin session to primary for N sec after write")
    print("  Routing strategies: round-robin (simple), least-conn (balanced),")
    print("    lag-aware (avoids stale replicas)")
    print("  Aurora: shared storage -> zero lag, up to 15 replicas")
```

quiz.question: How do you route reads to replicas — what strategies exist?
options: The reads aren't being routed to the replicas — they're still hitting the primary.
Unbounded lag means the replica can't keep up with the primary's WAL stream.
This is a textbook read-replica scenario — 1000:1 read-to-write ratio.
Four common routing strategies: (1) Round-robin — distribute reads evenly across replicas in a circular order.
quiz.explanation: Four common routing strategies: (1) Round-robin — distribute reads evenly across replicas in a circular order. Simple, stateless, no replica-specific metrics needed. Bad when replicas have different capacities or lags — a slow replica gets the same traffic as a fast one.

quiz.question: How does Amazon Aurora's replication differ from PostgreSQL streaming replication?
options: When the primary fails, one replica is promoted to be the new primary.
The reads aren't being routed to the replicas — they're still hitting the primary.
Read replicas don't help in several scenarios. (1) Write-heavy workloads — if writes are the bottleneck, replicas don't help (they only scale reads).
Traditional PostgreSQL: each replica has its own storage; the primary streams WAL to replicas, which apply it to their local storage.
quiz.explanation: Traditional PostgreSQL: each replica has its own storage; the primary streams WAL to replicas, which apply it to their local storage. Replicas lag by milliseconds to seconds depending on network and apply rate. Adding a replica requires copying data (or starting from a backup), taking minutes to hours. **Aurora: the storage layer is a distributed, replicated log across 6 copies (3 AZs × 2 copies).

quiz.question: What is replica lag and how do you monitor and mitigate it?
options: This is a classic "lagging replica after failover" or "round-robin routing during failover" issue.
Traditional PostgreSQL: each replica has its own storage; the primary streams WAL to replicas, which apply it to their local storage.
The reads aren't being routed to the replicas — they're still hitting the primary.
Replica lag is the time (or bytes of WAL) a replica is behind the primary.
quiz.explanation: Replica lag is the time (or bytes of WAL) a replica is behind the primary. Monitoring: PostgreSQL's pg_stat_replication view shows write_lag, flush_lag, replay_lag (time-based) and sent_lsn vs replay_lsn (byte-based). MySQL's SHOW REPLICA STATUS shows Seconds_Behind_Master.
